etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ton, tone, from Latin tonus (“sound, tone”) (possibly through Old French ton), from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos, “strain, tension, pitch”), from τείνω (teínō, “I stretch”). Doublet of tune, ton, tonos, and tonus.

definitions.definition: (music) A specific pitch.
(music) (in the diatonic scale) An interval of a major second.
(music) (in a Gregorian chant) A recitational melody.
The character of a sound, especially the timbre of an instrument or voice.
(language, linguistics) The pitch of a word's sound that distinguishes a difference in meaning, as for example in Chinese.
(language, dated) A whining style of speaking; a kind of mournful or artificial strain of voice; an affected speaking with a measured rhythm and a regular rise and fall of the voice.
(language, literature) The manner in which speech or writing is expressed, especially the aspects of diction (word choice), connotation, emotiveness, and register.

quote.citation: 1850, William Cullen Bryant, Letters of a Traveller:
quote.text: Their tone was dissatisfied, almost menacing.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) State of mind; temper; mood.

quote.citation: c. 1714 (undated), Henry St John, 1st Viscount Bolingbroke, letter to Alexander Pope
quote.text: The strange situation I am in and the melancholy state of public affairs,  […]  drag the mind down  […]  from a philosophical tone or temper, to the drudgery of private and public business.

definitions.definition: The shade or quality of a colour.

quote.citation: 2017, Adam Rutherford, A Brief History of Everyone Who Ever Lived, The Experiment, →ISBN, page 81:
quote.text: We make crude visual distinctions and effectively meaningless categorizations based on average skin tones, such as black or white.

definitions.definition: The favourable effect of a picture produced by the combination of light and shade, or of colours.
The definition and firmness of a muscle or organ; see also: tonus.
(biology) The state of a living body or of any of its organs or parts in which the functions are healthy and performed with due vigor.
(biology) Normal tension or responsiveness to stimuli.
(African-American Vernacular, slang) a gun

quote.citation: 1993, “9 Little Millimeta Boys”, in 8Ball (lyrics), Comin' Out Hard:
quote.text: But nigga don't step wrong, cuz 8ball keep a tone

quote.citation: 1994, “Murda In Da 1st Degree”, in Princess Loko (lyrics), Ashes 2 Ashes, Dust 2 Dust:
quote.text: M.A.C.T.D.O.G got the tone so hoe you know it's on

quote.citation: 2002, “Mouth Write a Check”, in Project Pat (lyrics), Layin' da Smack Down:
quote.text: Got the tone to ya head yo life flashing right front your eyes

definitions.definition: The general character, atmosphere, mood, or vibe (of a situation, place, etc.).

quote.citation: 2016 July 25, Megan McDermott, “'Repeal the 8th' mural in Project Arts Centre in Temple Bar removed”, in Irish Times‎[1]:
quote.text: Mr O'Brien confirmed the warning from the council was based on the fact that the structure the mural was painted on was not a temporary one and on the claim that it changes the tone of the street and impacts on the area.

quote.citation: 2016 December 30, Francine Kopun, “Sleepy Yonge and St. Clair gets a makeover”, in Toronto Star‎[2]:
quote.text: Manuel expects that once 2 St. Clair West is done it will change the tone of the neighbourhood.

quote.citation: 2022 December 2, “Many solutions, some small, needed to tackle addictions in the N.W.T.”, in CBC‎[3]:
quote.text: "What struck me most was not necessarily what was said but ... the tone of the room, ... the fear and anxiety that people have for their family members who are currently in the grip of addiction," Green said.

definitions.definition: (Chiefly in the form lower/raise the tone of something) The quality of being respectable or admirable.

quote.citation: 1904, May Sinclair, The Divine Fire, H. Holt, page 340:
quote.text: "I am going to raise the tone of the business. That's wot I want you for. To raise the tone of the business."

quote.citation: 1911, Charles Augustus Jenkens, The Bride's Return, Or, How Grand Avenue Church Came to Christ, C.H. Robinson, page 67:
quote.text: The teaching we have had of late has lowered the tone of Christianity, as the remarks by the two gentlemen who preceded me will attest; and, instead of producing stalwart manhood, it has generated a brood of mountebanks. Give us a pure Gospel or a vacant pulpit!

quote.citation: 2015 July 9, Simon Leo Brown, “St Kilda's Fitzroy Street left to rot says hotel owner”, in ABC News‎[4]:
quote.text: But Mr Fagan said the tone of the street was brought down by the presence of people he termed "the Gatwickians" — residents of a rooming house called the Gatwick Private Hotel.

quote.citation: 2016 July 11, Leah McLaren, “After Brexit, a political revolution in the U.K.—for women”, in Maclean's‎[5]:
quote.text: But for anyone hoping that what proved to be a brief two-way female Tory leadership race might have raised the tone of British politics—currently at an all-time low after the vicious backroom machinations of Brexit referendum—the news wasn't promising.

quote.citation: 2017 December 11, Michael Hann, “C7 bulbs or C9s? How Christmas lights became a nerdy obsession”, in The Guardian‎[6]:
quote.text: That story is replicated wherever there is a brightly decorated house and a neighbour who cares about the tone of the street.

definitions.definition: (figuratively)
(transitive) to give a particular tone to
(transitive) to change the colour of
(transitive) to make (something) firmer
(transitive) to utter with an affected tone.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English tone, ton, toon, from the incorrect division of thet one (“the/that one”). Compare Scots tane in the tane; see also tother.

definitions.definition: (now dialectal) the one (of two)
